title: What this lab is
text: The Virtual Neuro Lab runs experiments on simulated fruit fly (Drosophila) nervous systems wired from real connectome scans. Pages: Vivarium (the flies Maxime and Hagrid in 3D), Fly Atlas (brain regions and cell types), Chemicals (what substances do in real flies), Prediction check (how well the lab predicted anatomy), Experiments (Taste Bench, calibration, round 1 results, Discovery Screen). Experiments run on the FlyWire brain (female, 139,255 neurons, v783) using the published leaky integrate-and-fire model of Shiu et al. 2024 (Nature 634:210) with its published settings; rules for passing are saved before every run.

title: MN9 (tongue motor neuron)
text: MN9 is the motor neuron that extends the fly's proboscis (its tongue) to feed or drink. The lab reads MN9 firing as "tongue out" when it fires 10 or more times per second. There are two MN9s, one per side. Gordon & Scott 2009 (Neuron 61:373) showed it drives proboscis extension.

title: Usnea, Phantom, Fudog, Bract, Roundup, G2N-1 (named feeding neurons)
text: Named neurons in the fly's gnathal ganglion (the feeding centre under the brain) studied by Shiu et al. 2024 and earlier work. Usnea responds to water; Fudog responds to water; Bract and Roundup are needed for drinking; G2N-1 is not; Usnea and Phantom can drive proboscis extension when switched on.

title: Calibration test
text: Before any experiment, the simulated brain must reproduce a known result: sugar taste makes MN9 fire, more sugar more firing, bitter alone does not, bitter cancels sugar, water works, and activity stays contained. The FlyWire brain passed all six rules, so every experiment runs on it. Experiments on Maxime and Hagrid are in progress.

title: Pre-registration (rules saved before the run)
text: For every test the lab saves the question, the real-fly result, and the pass/fail rule with a timestamp before running. Nothing is changed after the run, and misses stay on the page. A fingerprint code on each card changes if the engine, wiring or rules are edited.

title: The simulation model (leaky integrate-and-fire)
text: Each neuron adds up pushes from the neurons wired to it; when its voltage crosses a threshold it fires and resets. Every synapse gives the same small push (0.275 mV), positive or negative depending on the sending neuron's chemical (GABA and glutamate inhibit). Published by Shiu et al. 2024 (Nature 634:210); in that study 91% of 164 predictions tested in living flies held up. Limits: no graded (non-spiking) neurons, no neuromodulators, no body.

title: Connectome, FlyWire, BANC, male CNS
text: A connectome is a map of every neuron and synapse, traced from electron-microscope scans. FlyWire (female brain, 139,255 neurons) is the brain the experiments run on. BANC (Maxime, female brain and nerve cord) and the male CNS (Hagrid, male brain and nerve cord) are the lab's two flies.

title: Region optic (Optic lobe)
text: optic Optic lobe: vision. The two big visual centres behind the eyes. Signals from the photoreceptors pass layer by layer through the lamina, medulla, lobula and lobula plate, which pull out contrast, colour, motion and object features before sending them on to the central brain. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 4463630}, Hagrid {'synapses': 31411837}.

title: Region LA (Lamina)
text: LA Lamina: first visual layer. The first layer behind the eye. Each of about 800 'cartridges' collects input from the R1–6 photoreceptors that look at one point in space and passes it to lamina neurons L1–L5. Counts: Maxime None, Hagrid {'synapses': 318834, 'neurons': 10762, 'left': 117415, 'right': 201419}.

title: Region ME (Medulla)
text: ME Medulla: early vision: contrast, colour, motion. The largest visual region, built of about 800 columns and ten layers. Colour photoreceptors R7 and R8 end here, and its circuits start computing contrast, colour and the direction of motion. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 2928364, 'neurons': 67228, 'left': 1184834, 'right': 1743530}, Hagrid {'synapses': 18681783, 'neurons': 85152, 'left': 8358660, 'right': 10323123}.

title: Region AME (Accessory medulla)
text: AME Accessory medulla: small optic region; clock-neuron hub. A small region at the front edge of the medulla. Clock neurons that make the neuropeptide PDF branch here and receive light information that helps reset the daily clock. The clock itself is a network of about 240 neurons spread across the brain (the count from the FlyWire connectome; older textbooks say about 150). Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 4139, 'neurons': 376, 'left': 1852, 'right': 2287}, Hagrid {'synapses': 27481, 'neurons': 505, 'left': 5703, 'right': 21778}.

title: Region LO (Lobula)
text: LO Lobula: visual features and objects. A deeper visual region that detects features such as small moving objects and looming. Its lobula columnar (LC) neurons carry these features to glomeruli in the central brain. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 831538, 'neurons': 37016, 'left': 360616, 'right': 470922}, Hagrid {'synapses': 8041134, 'neurons': 51998, 'left': 3481644, 'right': 4559490}.

title: Region LOP (Lobula plate)
text: LOP Lobula plate: direction of motion. Receives direction-selective motion signals from T4 and T5 cells, one layer per direction. Large tangential cells here sense whole-field motion (optic flow) used to keep the fly on course. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 699589, 'neurons': 21326, 'left': 296254, 'right': 403335}, Hagrid {'synapses': 4342605, 'neurons': 27083, 'left': 1850091, 'right': 2492514}.

title: Region AL (Antennal lobe)
text: AL Antennal lobe: smell, first stop. The first smell centre, with about 50 glomeruli. Each glomerulus collects the smell neurons that carry one type of odour receptor; projection neurons then carry the signal to the mushroom body and lateral horn. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 990557, 'neurons': 5683, 'left': 503736, 'right': 486821}, Hagrid {'synapses': 2918760, 'neurons': 4767, 'left': 1340846, 'right': 1577914}.

title: Region LH (Lateral horn)
text: LH Lateral horn: inborn smell responses. Receives smell information from the antennal lobe and drives built-in (unlearned) reactions, such as attraction to food odours or avoidance of danger smells. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 151180, 'neurons': 5085, 'left': 63964, 'right': 87216}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1032499, 'neurons': 6457, 'left': 451992, 'right': 580507}.

title: Region MB (Mushroom body)
text: MB Mushroom body: learning and memory. The fly's learning centre. Kenyon cells receive smell (and some visual and taste) information in the calyx and send long axons through the pedunculus into the lobes. There, dopamine neurons signal reward or punishment and output neurons read out the learned value. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 220993}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1713757}.

title: Region MB_CA (Mushroom body calyx)
text: MB_CA Mushroom body calyx: learning centre input. Where projection neurons carrying smell (and some visual and taste) information connect to the Kenyon cells of the mushroom body. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 180575, 'neurons': 5347, 'left': 86376, 'right': 94199}, Hagrid {'synapses': 456939, 'neurons': 4700, 'left': 209202, 'right': 247737}.

title: Region CX (Central complex)
text: CX Central complex: navigation and heading. A chain of midline structures that keep track of which way the fly is facing and help it steer toward goals. It holds the fly's internal compass. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 415870}, Hagrid {'synapses': 2180852}.

title: Region EB (Ellipsoid body)
text: EB Ellipsoid body: heading compass. A ring-shaped structure where E-PG neurons keep a 'bump' of activity that tracks the fly's heading, like an internal compass. Ring neurons bring in visual landmarks. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 112554, 'neurons': 690, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}, Hagrid {'synapses': 652120, 'neurons': 590, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}.

title: Region PB (Protocerebral bridge)
text: PB Protocerebral bridge: heading map relay. A bar-shaped structure where the heading signal from the ellipsoid body is laid out left-to-right and passed to other central-complex neurons. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 62377, 'neurons': 634, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}, Hagrid {'synapses': 158924, 'neurons': 770, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}.

title: Region FB (Fan-shaped body)
text: FB Fan-shaped body: goal-directed steering; sleep. The largest central-complex structure. It combines heading with travel direction and goals to guide steering, and some of its layers help control sleep. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 208450, 'neurons': 2895, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1201153, 'neurons': 2677, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}.

title: Region NO (Noduli)
text: NO Noduli: self-motion input. Small paired structures under the fan-shaped body that bring self-motion (speed and turning) signals into the central complex. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 32489, 'neurons': 529, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}, Hagrid {'synapses': 163428, 'neurons': 589, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}.

title: Region AB (Asymmetrical body)
text: AB Asymmetrical body: small, one-sided structure. A small structure near the fan-shaped body, usually larger on one side. It has been linked to long-term memory, but its role is not well understood. Counts: Maxime {'merged_into': 'FB'}, Hagrid {'synapses': 5227, 'neurons': 205, 'left': 943, 'right': 4284}.

title: Region LX (Lateral complex)
text: LX Lateral complex: steering; compass input. Paired regions next to the central complex. The bulb feeds visual cues into the compass, the gall links to compass neurons, and the lateral accessory lobe sends steering signals to descending neurons. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 378708}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1411129}.

title: Region LAL (Lateral accessory lobe)
text: LAL Lateral accessory lobe: steering commands. Receives central-complex output and connects to descending neurons that turn the fly while walking or flying. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 360381, 'neurons': 3949, 'left': 176652, 'right': 183729}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1375008, 'neurons': 5516, 'left': 727487, 'right': 647521}.

title: Region BU (Bulb)
text: BU Bulb: visual cues into the compass. Relays visual information such as landmarks, the sun and polarised light from the anterior optic tubercle to the ring neurons of the ellipsoid body. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 5343, 'neurons': 449, 'left': 2448, 'right': 2895}, Hagrid {'synapses': 36121, 'neurons': 589, 'left': 18003, 'right': 18118}.

title: Region GA (Gall)
text: GA Gall: compass-circuit partner. A small region where certain ellipsoid-body/protocerebral-bridge columnar neurons connect; part of the navigation loop. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 12984, 'neurons': 509, 'left': 5729, 'right': 7255}, Hagrid {'merged_into': 'LAL'}.

title: Region SNP (Superior neuropils)
text: SNP Superior neuropils: senses meet internal state. The top of the central brain, where smell, taste and other senses are combined with hunger, thirst and learned value. Many mushroom-body output and dopamine neurons connect here. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 407816}, Hagrid {'synapses': 4487271}.

title: Region SLP (Superior lateral protocerebrum)
text: SLP Superior lateral protocerebrum: smell and metabolic state. Next to the lateral horn. Receives smell information and links it with signals about the body's nutritional state. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 78770, 'neurons': 5410, 'left': 37358, 'right': 41412}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1763004, 'neurons': 11985, 'left': 815835, 'right': 947169}.

title: Region SIP (Superior intermediate protocerebrum)
text: SIP Superior intermediate protocerebrum: learned value. A zone where mushroom-body output neurons and dopamine neurons connect, linking learned value to behaviour. title: Region SMP (Superior medial protocerebrum)
text: SMP Superior medial protocerebrum: internal state and feeding. A large midline region that integrates hunger, thirst and other internal states with learned and sensory information; many neurosecretory and mushroom-body-related neurons connect here. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 273618, 'neurons': 6046, 'left': 132039, 'right': 141579}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1860508, 'neurons': 9125, 'left': 950400, 'right': 910108}.

title: Region CRE (Crepine)
text: CRE Crepine: around the mushroom-body lobes. Wraps the mushroom-body lobes and holds many mushroom-body output and dopamine neuron branches. title: Region VLNP (Ventrolateral neuropils)
text: VLNP Ventrolateral neuropils: visual and hearing features. text: AOTU Anterior optic tubercle: visual features to the compass. text: VMNP Ventromedial neuropils: routes to descending neurons. The lower middle of the central brain. text: BM_vOcci_vPoOr — bristle mechanosensory neuron: touch-sensing neuron of bristles on the head. The FlyWire reference brain has 52 of these cells (27 left, 25 right). Most of their synapses are in GNG. Transmitter: acetylcholine (predicted from images, 83% of the cells that have a prediction). Sensory: carries signals into the nervous system.

title: Cell type MTe01b
text: MTe01b — medulla tangential neuron: connects the medulla with the central brain; individual roles are mostly unknown. The FlyWire reference brain has 48 of these cells (23 left, 25 right). Most of their synapses are in ME, SPS, IPS. Transmitter: acetylcholine (predicted from images, 100% of the cells that have a prediction). (The 3D view shows the 52 cells that the Codex export labels MTe01b.) Stays inside the brain (it can still connect several regions).

title: Cell type ORN_DM6
text: ORN_DM6 — olfactory receptor neuron, glomerulus DM6: smell neuron in the antenna or palp; all neurons of one type carry the same odour receptor and meet in one antennal-lobe glomerulus. The FlyWire reference brain has 52 of these cells (27 left, 25 right). Most of their synapses are in AL. Transmitter: acetylcholine (confirmed in experiments). Sensory: carries signals into the nervous system.

title: Cell type Li09
text: Li09 — lobula intrinsic neuron: local cell inside the lobula. The FlyWire reference brain has 52 of these cells (26 left, 26 right). Most of their synapses are in LO. Transmitter: GABA (predicted from images, 100% of the cells that have a prediction). Stays inside the brain (it can still connect several regions).

title: Cell type ORN_DL4
text: ORN_DL4 — olfactory receptor neuron, glomerulus DL4: smell neuron in the antenna or palp; all neurons of one type carry the same odour receptor and meet in one antennal-lobe glomerulus (Or49a/Or85f; senses odours of parasitic wasps). The FlyWire reference brain has 52 of these cells (27 left, 25 right). Most of their synapses are in AL. Transmitter: acetylcholine (confirmed in experiments). Sensory: carries signals into the nervous system.

title: Cell type Pm06
text: Pm06 — proximal medulla neuron: local cell that spreads across several columns of the inner medulla. The FlyWire reference brain has 51 of these cells (26 left, 25 right). Most of their synapses are in ME. Transmitter: GABA (confirmed in experiments). Stays inside the brain (it can still connect several regions).

title: Cell type cLP01
text: cLP01 — centrifugal lobula plate neuron: carries signals from the central brain back into the lobula plate. The FlyWire reference brain has 51 of these cells. Most of their synapses are in LOP, IPS. Transmitter: GABA (predicted from images, 100% of the cells that have a prediction). Stays inside the brain (it can still connect several regions).

title: Chemical: Caffeine
text: Caffeine (C8H10N4O2; scientific name: 1,3,7-trimethylpurine-2,6-dione). The stimulant in coffee, tea and energy drinks. In flies: Flies given caffeine sleep less, especially at night. Surprisingly, this does not need the fly's adenosine receptor (caffeine's main target in people). It needs PKA (a cAMP-driven signalling enzyme) and dopamine made by a cluster of brain cells called the PAM neurons. Flies also taste caffeine as bitter and avoid eating it. Route: Eaten (mixed into food); tasted on the legs and mouthparts. Targets: PAM dopamine neurons (carry the wake-up effect); Gr66a, Gr33a, Gr93a (bitter taste receptors that detect caffeine); AdoR (the fly's only adenosine receptor - not needed for the sleep effect). Confidence: fly. Papers: Nall et al. (2016) Sci Rep 6:20938: caffeine promotes wakefulness via dopamine and PAM neurons, independently of the adenosine receptor; Wu et al. (2009) J Neurosci 29:11029: caffeine's effect on fly sleep requires PKA activity but not the adenosine receptor; Moon et al. (2006) Curr Biol 16:1812: Gr66a is required for the caffeine taste response; Lee, Moon & Montell (2009) PNAS 106:4495: several gustatory receptors, including Gr93a, are needed to detect caffeine

title: Chemical: Theophylline
text: Theophylline (C7H8N4O2; scientific name: 1,3-dimethyl-7H-purine-2,6-dione). A caffeine relative used as an asthma medicine; tea contains only trace amounts. In flies: No fruit-fly study is on file. In people it blocks adenosine receptors (more strongly than caffeine) and, at higher doses, the enzyme that breaks down cAMP. Because caffeine's wake effect in flies runs through cAMP and dopamine rather than the adenosine receptor, the mammal ranking may not carry over to flies. Route: Eaten. Targets: unknown in flies (adenosine receptors and phosphodiesterase in mammals). Confidence: mammal. Papers: Fredholm & Sandberg (1983) Br J Pharmacol 80:639: adenosine-receptor potency theophylline > caffeine > theobromine (mammalian)

title: Chemical: Theobromine
text: Theobromine (C7H8N4O2; scientific name: 3,7-dimethyl-1H-purine-2,6-dione). The caffeine relative in chocolate and cocoa. In flies: No fruit-fly study is on file. In people it is a weaker adenosine blocker than caffeine. As with theophylline, the mammal ranking may not carry over to flies, because caffeine works in flies through cAMP and dopamine instead. Route: Eaten. Targets: unknown in flies (adenosine receptors in mammals). Confidence: mammal. Papers: Fredholm & Sandberg (1983) Br J Pharmacol 80:639: adenosine-receptor potency theophylline > caffeine > theobromine (mammalian)

title: Chemical: Nicotine
text: Nicotine (C10H14N2; scientific name: 3-[(2S)-1-methylpyrrolidin-2-yl]pyridine). The addictive chemical in tobacco. Plants make it as a natural insecticide. In flies: Nicotine switches on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which carry most of the fast 'go' signals between nerve cells in the fly brain. Flies exposed to nicotine vapour first become hyperactive, then uncoordinated, and at higher doses stop moving. The fly's dopamine system shapes how strongly it reacts. Route: Breathed in as vapour, or eaten. Targets: nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (the fly brain's main fast excitatory receptors). Confidence: fly. Papers: Bainton et al. (2000) Curr Biol 10:187: dopamine modulates acute responses to cocaine, nicotine and ethanol in Drosophila

title: Chemical: Imidacloprid
text: Imidacloprid (C9H10ClN5O2; scientific name: N-[1-[(6-chloropyridin-3-yl)methyl]-4,5-dihydroimidazol-2-yl]nitramide). A neonicotinoid insecticide, widely used on crops. In flies: It grips the same nicotinic acetylcholine receptors as nicotine, but far more tightly in insects than in mammals, which is what makes it an insecticide. Low doses disturb movement and behaviour; high doses cause paralysis and death. Route: Eaten or by contact. Targets: nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (binds them very tightly in insects). Confidence: fly. Papers: Zhang et al. (2000) J Neurochem 75:1294: imidacloprid binds acetylcholine receptors from Drosophila heads

title: Chemical: Aldicarb
text: Aldicarb (C7H14N2O2S; scientific name: [(E)-(2-methyl-2-methylsulfanylpropylidene)amino] N-methylcarbamate). A carbamate insecticide, now heavily restricted. In flies: It blocks acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that clears acetylcholine away after each signal. Acetylcholine piles up, nerve cells are over-stimulated, and the fly goes from tremors and loss of coordination to paralysis and death. It is a poison, not a stimulant. Route: Eaten or by contact. Targets: Ace (acetylcholinesterase) (the enzyme it blocks). Confidence: insect. Papers: Xu et al. (2007) Biomol Eng 24:253: engineered Drosophila acetylcholinesterase used to detect organophosphate and carbamate pesticides

title: Chemical: Muscarine
text: Muscarine (C9H20NO2+; scientific name: [(2S,4R,5S)-4-hydroxy-5-methyloxolan-2-yl]methyl-trimethylazanium). A mushroom toxin found in Inocybe and Clitocybe mushrooms. It was first isolated from the fly agaric, which contains only traces. In flies: It switches on muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, mainly the A-type. In flies these are slow 'tuning' receptors, not the main fast signal; the A-type, for example, works in the mushroom body during learning. So muscarine should change how circuits are tuned rather than simply turning brain activity up. (Receptor responses were measured on fly receptors grown in cultured cells.) Route: Eaten. Targets: mAChR-A (strongly activated); mAChR-B (responds only weakly (about 1,000-fold less sensitive)); mAChR-C (not tested). Confidence: fly. Papers: Collin et al. (2013) Cell Mol Life Sci 70:3231: muscarine strongly activates the fly A-type muscarinic receptor; the B-type is far less sensitive (tested in cultured cells); Bielopolski et al. (2019) eLife 8:e48264: muscarinic receptor mAChR-A in mushroom-body neurons is needed for aversive olfactory learning

title: Chemical: Atropine
text: Atropine (C17H23NO3; scientific name: (8-methyl-8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octan-3-yl) 3-hydroxy-2-phenylpropanoate). A drug from deadly nightshade, used by doctors to widen pupils and speed up the heart. In flies: It blocks muscarinic receptors. Flies have three types: the A-type is blocked by atropine, the B-type is not, and the C-type has not been tested. It does not block the fast nicotinic signals that carry most of the traffic in the fly brain. Route: Eaten. Targets: mAChR-A (blocked); mAChR-B (not blocked); mAChR-C (not tested). Confidence: fly. Papers: Collin et al. (2013) Cell Mol Life Sci 70:3231: Drosophila has A- and B-type muscarinic receptors; classic blockers such as atropine and scopolamine block the A-type but not the B-type

title: Chemical: Scopolamine
text: Scopolamine (C17H21NO4; scientific name: (9-methyl-3-oxa-9-azatricyclo[3.3.1.0²,⁴]nonan-7-yl) 3-hydroxy-2-phenylpropanoate). A nightshade-plant drug used against motion sickness. In flies: Like atropine, it blocks the fly's A-type muscarinic receptor but not the B-type (the C-type is untested), and leaves the fast nicotinic signals alone. Route: Eaten. Targets: mAChR-A (blocked); mAChR-B (not blocked); mAChR-C (not tested). Confidence: fly. Papers: Collin et al. (2013) Cell Mol Life Sci 70:3231: Drosophila has A- and B-type muscarinic receptors; classic blockers such as atropine and scopolamine block the A-type but not the B-type

title: Chemical: Picrotoxin
text: Picrotoxin (C30H34O13; scientific name: an equal mixture of picrotoxinin (C15H16O6) and picrotin (C15H18O7)). A plant poison that causes convulsions. In flies: It blocks the fly's main 'brake' receptor, the GABA-gated chloride channel called Rdl. In flies it also blocks glutamate-gated chloride channels, because glutamate acts as a calming signal in parts of the fly brain. So it removes two brakes at once. A single change in Rdl makes flies resistant to it and to some insecticides. Route: Eaten, or applied to the brain in recordings. Targets: Rdl (GABA receptor (main inhibitory brake)); GluClα (glutamate-gated chloride channel (second brake)). Confidence: fly. Papers: ffrench-Constant et al. (1993) Nature 363:449: a point mutation in the Drosophila Rdl GABA receptor confers resistance to picrotoxin and dieldrin; Liu & Wilson (2013) PNAS 110:10294: glutamate is an inhibitory transmitter in the fly olfactory system via GluClα, blocked by picrotoxin

title: Chemical: Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)
text: Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ) (C6H10N4; scientific name: 6,7,8,9-tetrahydro-5H-tetrazolo[1,5-a]azepine). A drug used in labs to trigger seizures. In flies: In mammals it blocks GABA-A 'brake' receptors. Flies fed it are used as a seizure and brain-plasticity model, though its exact target in the fly is less well defined. Route: Eaten. Targets: Rdl (probable) (GABA receptor, by analogy with mammals). Confidence: fly. Papers: Mohammad, Singh & Sharma (2009) BMC Syst Biol 3:11: Drosophila PTZ feeding model of seizure-related plasticity

title: Chemical: Phenobarbital
text: Phenobarbital (C12H12N2O3; scientific name: 5-ethyl-5-phenyl-1,3-diazinane-2,4,6-trione). An old sleep and anti-seizure medicine (a barbiturate). In flies: In mammals it strengthens the GABA 'brake'. In flies it is best known for something else, shown directly in flies: it switches on detox genes (cytochrome P450s) through the CncC pathway. Its sedating effect in flies is borrowed from mammal studies. Route: Eaten. Targets: CncC / Maf-S (switches on detox genes (shown in flies)); Rdl (GABA receptor (by analogy with mammals)). Confidence: mammal. Papers: Misra et al. (2011) Genes Dev 25:1796: CncC/Maf drives the fly's transcriptional response to phenobarbital

title: Chemical: Vigabatrin
text: Vigabatrin (C6H11NO2; scientific name: 4-aminohex-5-enoic acid). An epilepsy medicine. In flies: It permanently blocks GABA transaminase, the enzyme that breaks GABA down, so GABA builds up. Flies have the same enzyme (Gabat); flies missing it have two to three times more brain GABA and sleep more, the best clue to what the drug would do. Recovery needs new enzyme, which takes days. Route: Eaten. Targets: Gabat (GABA transaminase) (the enzyme it blocks). Confidence: mammal. Papers: Ben-Menachem (2011) Acta Neurol Scand 124(Suppl 192):5: vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase (mammalian review); Chen et al. (2015) Mol Psychiatry 20:240: flies lacking GABA transaminase have raised brain GABA and more sleep

title: Chemical: Isoflurane
text: Isoflurane (C3H2ClF5O; scientific name: 2-chloro-2-(difluoromethoxy)-1,1,1-trifluoroethane). A gas anaesthetic used in surgery. In flies: Flies breathing it are knocked out and recover once it is removed. Fly genetics has shown that the brain's sleep–wake circuits change how sensitive a fly is to it. Route: Breathed in as a gas. Targets: several (no single target; sleep–wake circuits set sensitivity). Confidence: fly. Papers: Kottler et al. (2013) Curr Biol 23:594: a sleep/wake circuit controls isoflurane sensitivity in Drosophila

title: Chemical: Ethanol
text: Ethanol (C2H6O; scientific name: ethanol). Drinking alcohol. In flies: Flies respond much like people: a short burst of hyperactivity, then loss of coordination, then sedation. With repeated exposure they become tolerant, and they can come to prefer alcohol-laced food. Route: Breathed in as vapour, or eaten. Targets: several (GABA receptors, dopamine signalling and more). Confidence: fly. Papers: Wolf et al. (2002) J Neurosci 22:11035: ethanol first stimulates then sedates Drosophila locomotion; Devineni & Heberlein (2009) Curr Biol 19:2126: flies come to prefer ethanol-containing food, with features of addiction

title: Chemical: Tetrodotoxin (TTX)
text: Tetrodotoxin (TTX) (C11H17N3O8; scientific name: a guanidinium alkaloid (aminoperhydroquinazoline) from the bacteria that live in pufferfish). The pufferfish poison. In flies: It plugs voltage-gated sodium channels. In flies that channel is made by the para gene. Without it, nerve cells cannot fire, and the result is paralysis. Fly labs use it to silence nerve signals during recordings. Route: Injected or applied to tissue. Targets: para (the fly's voltage-gated sodium channel). Confidence: fly. Papers: Warmke et al. (1997) J Gen Physiol 110:119: the Drosophila para sodium channel, expressed in oocytes, is blocked by tetrodotoxin

title: Chemical: Tetanus toxin
text: Tetanus toxin (protein; scientific name: tetanospasmin, a zinc protease made by the bacterium Clostridium tetani). The bacterial toxin behind tetanus (lockjaw). In flies: It cuts synaptobrevin, a protein nerve cells need to release their signals. In flies it is not fed: researchers make chosen nerve cells produce it, as a genetic tool to switch those cells' outputs off. The cells still fire, but no chemical signal reaches the next cell. Route: Made inside chosen cells (genetic tool). Targets: n-Syb (neuronal synaptobrevin) (the release protein it cuts). Confidence: fly. Papers: Sweeney et al. (1995) Neuron 14:341: targeted tetanus-toxin light chain blocks synaptic transmission in Drosophila

title: Chemical: Permethrin
text: Permethrin (C21H20Cl2O3; scientific name: (3-phenoxyphenyl)methyl 3-(2,2-dichloroethenyl)-2,2-dimethylcyclopropane-1-carboxylate). A pyrethroid insecticide used on clothing, pets and crops. In flies: It holds the para sodium channel open, so nerve cells fire over and over. Flies show 'knockdown' (twitching and falling over), then paralysis. Changes in the para gene, the 'kdr' mutations, make flies resistant. Route: By contact or eaten. Targets: para (the sodium channel it holds open). Confidence: fly. Papers: Soderlund et al. (2002) Toxicology 171:3: pyrethroids act on insect sodium channels; Pittendrigh et al. (1997) Mol Gen Genet 256:602: para sodium-channel mutations give pyrethroid resistance in Drosophila

title: Chemical: Paraquat
text: Paraquat (C12H14N2²⁺ (sold as the dichloride salt, C12H14Cl2N2); scientific name: 1,1′-dimethyl-4,4′-bipyridine-1,1′-diium). A weed-killer, banned in many countries. In flies: It produces damaging reactive oxygen inside cells. Flies fed paraquat develop movement problems and die early, so it is widely used as an oxidative-stress test and a Parkinson's-like model. Some labs report the loss of particular dopamine neurons; others do not see it. Route: Eaten. Targets: mitochondria and other cell machinery (oxidative damage); dopamine neurons (reported as especially vulnerable in some studies). Confidence: fly. Papers: Chaudhuri et al. (2007) J Neurosci 27:2457: paraquat causes dopamine-neuron loss and parkinsonian symptoms in Drosophila; Navarro et al. (2014) J Neurochem 131:369: no dopamine-neuron loss found in several fly Parkinson's models, paraquat included

title: Chemical: Amphetamine
text: Amphetamine (C9H13N; scientific name: 1-phenylpropan-2-amine). A stimulant medicine. In flies: It works through the fly's dopamine transporter (DAT). It runs the transporter backwards, so dopamine leaks out of nerve endings, and flies become more active. Fly larvae lacking DAT don't speed up on it. Route: Eaten. Targets: DAT (dopamine transporter) (reversed by amphetamine). Confidence: fly. Papers: Pizzo et al. (2013) Mol Psychiatry 18:824: amphetamine's effect on movement needs the dopamine transporter (shown in fly larvae); Freyberg et al. (2016) Nat Commun 7:10652: amphetamine's effect on dopamine vesicles observed in the Drosophila brain

title: Chemical: Cocaine
text: Cocaine (C17H21NO4; scientific name: methyl (1R,2R,3S,5S)-3-benzoyloxy-8-methyl-8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane-2-carboxylate). A stimulant from coca leaves. In flies: It blocks the dopamine transporter, so dopamine lingers at the cells that receive it. Flies show a dose-dependent sequence: extra grooming, then hyperactivity and circling, and at high doses they stop moving altogether. Repeat doses make them more sensitive. Route: Breathed in as vapour (free-base), or eaten. Targets: DAT (dopamine transporter) (blocked). Confidence: fly. Papers: McClung & Hirsh (1998) Curr Biol 8:109: stereotyped, dose-dependent cocaine behaviours and sensitisation in Drosophila; Bainton et al. (2000) Curr Biol 10:187: dopamine modulates acute cocaine responses in Drosophila

title: Chemical: Bupropion
text: Bupropion (C13H18ClNO; scientific name: 2-(tert-butylamino)-1-(3-chlorophenyl)propan-1-one). An antidepressant and quit-smoking medicine. In flies: In people it slows the clearing of dopamine and noradrenaline and weakly blocks nicotinic receptors. Flies have a dopamine transporter it could act on, but no noradrenaline; octopamine plays that role. No direct fruit-fly study is on file. Route: Eaten. Targets: DAT (probable) (dopamine transporter, by analogy with mammals). Confidence: mammal. Papers: Stahl et al. (2004) Prim Care Companion J Clin Psychiatry 6:159: bupropion inhibits dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake (mammalian); Slemmer, Martin & Damaj (2000) J Pharmacol Exp Ther 295:321: bupropion blocks nicotinic receptors (mammalian)

title: Chemical: Dopamine
text: Dopamine (C8H11NO2; scientific name: 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzene-1,2-diol). One of the fly's own brain signals, for reward, punishment and wakefulness. In flies: Different dopamine neurons signal reward or punishment for learning, and dopamine keeps flies awake. What it does depends on the receiving receptor: Dop1R1 and Dop1R2 generally excite, Dop2R calms, and DopEcR also responds to a steroid hormone. To raise brain dopamine, researchers usually feed its building block, L-DOPA, rather than dopamine itself. Route: Made in the brain; raised experimentally by feeding L-DOPA. Targets: Dop1R1, Dop1R2 (excite the receiving cell); Dop2R (calms the receiving cell); DopEcR (dopamine and steroid-hormone receptor). Confidence: fly. Papers: Yamamoto & Seto (2014) Exp Anim 63:107: review of Drosophila dopamine genes, receptors, drugs and behaviours; Kume et al. (2005) J Neurosci 25:7377: dopamine controls arousal and sleep in Drosophila (DAT mutant fumin)

title: Chemical: Octopamine
text: Octopamine (C8H11NO2; scientific name: 4-(2-amino-1-hydroxyethyl)phenol). The fly's own 'fight-or-flight' signal, its version of noradrenaline. In flies: It raises arousal, activity and energy use, and is needed for normal flight, egg-laying and aggression. It acts on several receptors and also travels in the blood as a hormone. Route: Made in the brain; released into synapses and the blood. Targets: OAMB (Octα1R) (receptor); Octα2R (receptor); Octβ1R, Octβ2R, Octβ3R (receptors); Oct-TyrR (also responds to tyramine). Confidence: fly. Papers: Roeder (2005) Annu Rev Entomol 50:447: octopamine as the insect arousal amine and hormone

title: Chemical: DEET
text: DEET (C12H17NO; scientific name: N,N-diethyl-3-methylbenzamide). The most common insect repellent. In flies: Flies avoid DEET mainly by taste. It switches on avoidance (bitter) taste neurons through the receptors Gr32a, Gr33a and Gr66a, and flies with no sense of smell still refuse DEET-laced food. DEET also acts on smell neurons, but exactly how is still debated. Route: Tasted on contact; also smelled. Targets: Gr32a, Gr33a, Gr66a (avoidance taste receptors that DEET switches on); Orco (smell co-receptor; DEET's effect here is debated); Ir40a (proposed DEET smell receptor (disputed)). Confidence: fly. Papers: Lee, Kim & Montell (2010) Neuron 67:555: DEET activates avoidance taste neurons via Gr32a, Gr33a and Gr66a; smell is not required; Ditzen, Pellegrino & Vosshall (2008) Science 319:1838: DEET inhibits Orco-dependent odour responses (later debated); Kain et al. (2013) Nature 502:507: Ir40a proposed as a DEET-sensing olfactory receptor (later disputed)

title: Chemical: Picaridin
text: Picaridin (C12H23NO3; scientific name: butan-2-yl 2-(2-hydroxyethyl)piperidine-1-carboxylate). A modern insect repellent. In flies: Mosquito studies show it changes how smell receptors respond. No direct fruit-fly study is on file. Route: Smelled; on contact. Targets: odorant receptors (mosquito) (responses altered). Confidence: insect. Papers: Bohbot & Dickens (2010) PLoS ONE 5:e12138: picaridin and DEET modulate mosquito odorant receptors

title: Chemical: Citronellal
text: Citronellal (C10H18O; scientific name: 3,7-dimethyloct-6-enal). The lemony smell in citronella and lemongrass oil. In flies: Flies avoid its smell. That avoidance needs both the smell co-receptor Orco and the TRPA1 channel in smell neurons. Route: Smelled. Targets: Orco (smell co-receptor); TRPA1 (irritant channel in smell neurons). Confidence: fly. Papers: Kwon et al. (2010) Curr Biol 20:1672: fly TRPA1 in smell neurons is required to avoid citronellal

title: Chemical: PMD (oil of lemon eucalyptus)
text: PMD (oil of lemon eucalyptus) (C10H20O2; scientific name: 2-(2-hydroxypropan-2-yl)-5-methylcyclohexan-1-ol). The active ingredient of refined oil of lemon eucalyptus repellents. In flies: Mosquitoes smell it and avoid it, and it triggers responses in their smell neurons. Fruit-fly studies are thin. Route: Smelled. Targets: smell neurons (mosquito) (respond to PMD). Confidence: insect. Papers: Afify & Potter (2020) Malaria J 19:127: PMD repels three mosquito species and triggers olfactory nerve responses

title: Chemical: Cinnamaldehyde
text: Cinnamaldehyde (C9H8O; scientific name: (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enal). The flavour and smell of cinnamon. In flies: In mammals cinnamaldehyde switches on TRPA1, an irritant-sensing channel. Flies have TRPA1 in their bitter taste neurons, where it senses reactive irritants like this one, so flies probably taste it as unpleasant. A fly test of cinnamaldehyde itself is not on file. Route: Tasted. Targets: TRPA1 (irritant channel in bitter taste neurons (expected target)). Confidence: mammal. Papers: Bandell et al. (2004) Neuron 41:849: cinnamaldehyde activates mammalian TRPA1; Kang et al. (2010) Nature 464:597: fly TRPA1 in taste neurons senses reactive irritants

title: Chemical: Camphor
text: Camphor (C10H16O; scientific name: 1,7,7-trimethylbicyclo[2.2.1]heptan-2-one). The strong cooling smell in vapour rubs. In flies: In mammals it activates TRPV1 and blocks TRPA1. Flies can smell it, but direct fly studies of how it acts are thin. Route: Smelled. Targets: unknown in flies (TRPV1 / TRPA1 in mammals). Confidence: mammal. Papers: Xu, Blair & Clapham (2005) J Neurosci 25:8924: camphor activates TRPV1 and inhibits TRPA1 (mammalian)

title: Chemical: Piperine
text: Piperine (C17H19NO3; scientific name: (2E,4E)-5-(1,3-benzodioxol-5-yl)-1-piperidin-1-ylpenta-2,4-dien-1-one). The hot compound in black pepper. In flies: In mammals it activates the TRPV1 and TRPA1 'spice' channels. Flies have no direct match for mammalian TRPV1, so its fly target is unknown. Route: Tasted or smelled. Targets: unknown in flies (TRPV1 / TRPA1 in mammals). Confidence: mammal. Papers: Aloum et al. (2021) Molecules 26:1627: review: piperine activates TRPV1 and TRPA1 (mammalian)

title: Chemical: Eugenol
text: Eugenol (C10H12O2; scientific name: 2-methoxy-4-prop-2-enylphenol). The smell of cloves. In flies: Studies in cockroaches and ants, and on insect receptors grown in cultured cells, suggest it acts on octopamine receptors. This has not been shown in living fruit flies, which mainly meet it as a smell. Route: Smelled. Targets: octopamine receptors (cockroach, ant) (proposed, not confirmed in flies). Confidence: insect. Papers: Enan (2001) Comp Biochem Physiol C 130:325: eugenol acts via octopamine receptors in insects

title: Chemical: Limonene
text: Limonene (C10H16; scientific name: 1-methyl-4-prop-1-en-2-ylcyclohexene). The main smell in orange and lemon peel. In flies: Flies smell it through Or19a smell neurons, which respond to citrus smells (most strongly valencene, and also limonene) and help females choose citrus fruit for laying eggs. Claims that limonene blocks acetylcholinesterase come from weak effects in grain pests, not flies. Route: Smelled. Targets: Or19a (citrus smell receptor (valencene first, limonene too)). Confidence: fly. Papers: Dweck et al. (2013) Curr Biol 23:2472: Or19a neurons respond to citrus terpenes (valencene, limonene) and guide egg-laying on citrus

title: Chemical: Sucrose
text: Sucrose (C12H22O11; scientific name: β-D-fructofuranosyl α-D-glucopyranoside). Table sugar. In flies: Sweet taste neurons on the legs and mouthparts detect it through the Gr5a and Gr64 receptor family. Flies find it attractive, and it is food. Route: Tasted and eaten. Targets: Gr5a, Gr64 family (sweet taste receptors). Confidence: fly. Papers: Dahanukar et al. (2007) Neuron 56:503: two Gr genes underlie sugar reception in Drosophila

title: Chemical: Sodium chloride
text: Sodium chloride (NaCl; scientific name: sodium chloride). Table salt. In flies: Low salt is attractive and high salt is avoided. Low salt is sensed by sweet taste cells using the receptor Ir56b with the helper receptors Ir25a and Ir76b. High salt is sensed by bitter cells and by dedicated high-salt cells that use Ir7c (with the same helpers). Route: Tasted and eaten. title: What we infer and why it matters (Taste experiments)
text: id="infer">What we infer, and why it matters What these results tell us Much of taste behaviour is written in the wiring. With nothing but the scanned connections and one simple rule for how neurons fire, the brain gets the basics right: sugar brings the tongue out, more sugar pushes harder, bitter alone does nothing, and water works through its own neurons. Bitter is built to win. In the bench, bitter cuts the sugar response from 65 to 0.1 firings a second, and with strong bitter, even double-strength sugar barely gets through (11 a second). A "safety first" design, which makes sense: tasting poison should overrule wanting food. Signals add up. Sugar and water together push the tongue neuron harder than either alone (83 vs 65 for sugar). Wiring isn't the whole story. The brain passed 10 of 15 checks. Results driven by whole groups of sensory neurons came out right; the misses all involve single named neurons. Something beyond the wiring, such as chemical signals for hunger or thirst, seems to shape those. How this can help in the real world Fewer animal experiments. A brain that passes known checks can be used to try ideas first, so real labs only test the most promising ones. The Knockout Lab does exactly this. Trust, measured. Brain simulations are becoming a common research tool. Scoring one honestly against known results, misses included, shows when its predictions are worth acting on. How brains weigh reward against danger. The bitter-beats-sugar rule is a simple, fully mapped example of a decision every animal makes. Flies are widely used to study how brains work because so much of their biology is shared with ours: most genes linked to human disease have a counterpart in the fly (Reiter et al. 2001, Genome Research ). Insect feeding. Knowing which taste signals stop an insect from eating is the basis of feeding deterrents. Whether this fly's wiring carries over to pest species would need testing in those species. What it doesn't tell us. This is a model of one female fly's brain, with no body, no hunger or thirst state and no chemical messengers. It shows what the wiring can do, not everything a living fly does.

title: What we infer and why it matters (Knockout Lab)
text: id="infer">What we infer, and why it matters What these results tell us The feeding circuit has backups. Of 286 neurons switched off one at a time, only 8 lowered the tongue signal by more than 20%. For most neurons the signal simply finds another way to the tongue. That kind of redundancy is how a brain stays working when single cells fail. Drinking has more bottlenecks than eating. 7 of the 8 "needed" neurons matter for water, only 2 for sugar. In this brain, the sugar signal travels on many parallel roads; the water signal leans on a few key cells. A few cells are true chokepoints. Switching off "Roundup" #2 nearly silences drinking (98% drop) and "Clavicle" cuts it by 84%. In the map you can see the route collapse. Three new candidates. CB0192, CB0051 and CB0501 are predicted to be needed for drinking, and we found no living-fly test of them. These are new, testable predictions. How this can help in the real world Where to look first. Testing every neuron in a living fly takes years. A screen like this narrows 286 candidates down to 3 untested ones a lab could check next, saving time and animals. A method that scales. The same switch-off-and-watch approach works for any behaviour with a known motor neuron, and for any other brain once it has been mapped. Understanding thirst. Knowing which few cells carry the "drink" signal helps explain how brains control fluid intake, a basic survival system every animal shares in some form. What it doesn't tell us. These are predictions, not facts. When we checked this brain against known results it scored 10 of 15, and its misses were exactly this kind of single-neuron question. Each of the 8 is a strong lead that still needs a living-fly experiment.

title: The worm (C. elegans), second organism
text: The lab's second organism is the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, about 1 mm long, the first animal whose complete wiring diagram was mapped. Every adult hermaphrodite has the same 302 named neurons. The Worm page shows all 302 in 3D with every neuron-to-neuron connection: 2,973 chemical links and 849 pairs joined by electrical links (gap junctions). Neurons are sensory (blue), interneurons (amber), motor (pink) or role unknown. Click a neuron to see who it sends to and receives from. Famous circuits: gentle touch (Chalfie et al. 1985: front touch neurons ALM and AVM feed AVD and AVA, which drive backing up; back touch neurons PLM feed PVC and AVB, which drive forward movement) and the nerve ring hubs (AIB, AIY, AIZ, RIA, RIM, AVA, AVB). Data: neuron shapes from the Virtual Worm 3D model by Grove and Sternberg (WormBase, Caltech, public domain), converted to NeuroML by OpenWorm (c302, MIT licence); the shapes are a hand-built model matched to known anatomy, not traced from one scan. Wiring: Cook et al. 2019, Nature 571:63, as packaged by OpenWorm c302. Experiments on the worm are in progress; they need their own calibration test against real-worm results first.
